Part 1 · One system, five spheres
01Push one, and the rest moveActivity 13.1 · the five spheres45 XP

The Earth is not five separate subjects. It is one system of interacting spheres, and a disturbance in any one of them travels to the others. Tap a sphere, then set a disturbance running.

Sphere
—
In India
—
Touches
—
Five spheres, and every one of them shares a boundary with the others. Nothing here can be changed on its own.

The geosphere is solid rock, soil, landforms and the Earth's interior — the Deccan plateau, the Thar desert. The hydrosphere is liquid water: oceans, rivers like the Ganga–Brahmaputra system, lakes and groundwater. The cryosphere is water as ice and snow — Himalayan glaciers, snow in Ladakh, the polar caps. The atmosphere is the air around the Earth. The biosphere is every living organism and its habitat, from mangroves to ocean plankton to coral reefs.

A few years of less snowfall means less meltwater in the lake by summer, so less water for the grass, so less grazing for the sheep — cryosphere to hydrosphere to biosphere. On a larger scale, warmer Arabian Sea water means more evaporation, which drives the southwest monsoon, which brings floods to some regions of India and drought to others.

02Which sphere is it?Section 13.0 · sorting the examples35 XP

Tap an example, then tap the sphere it belongs to.

Notice how many of these could have been argued into a second sphere. A glacier is water, but frozen, so it is cryosphere rather than hydrosphere. Groundwater is underground, but liquid, so it is hydrosphere rather than geosphere. The boundaries are conventions that make the system easier to talk about — not walls.

Part 2 · The energy that drives it
03What the Sun actually sendsSection 13.1 · Fig. 13.240 XP

Solar radiation arrives as electromagnetic waves, which travel through a vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ — unlike sound waves, which need a medium. Slide across the spectrum and see which parts get through.

Band
—
Reaches the surface
—
What it does
—
High frequency means short wavelength and high energy. Slide from gamma rays on the left to radio waves on the right.

About 99 per cent of the Sun's energy falls in the ultraviolet, visible and infrared range, and it is these three regions that shape the Earth's climate and support life. Gamma rays and X-rays are mostly filtered out by the upper atmosphere; microwaves and radio waves carry too little energy to warm the Earth appreciably.

UV: 100 to 400 nanometres
One nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m. UV rays carry much more energy than visible light, and prolonged exposure damages the eyes and skin and raises the risk of cancer — hence sunglasses and sunscreen. The same energy makes UV useful for killing germs in water purifiers and for powering fluorescent lights.
04How much energy actually arrivesExample 13.1 · the solar constant50 XP

The solar constant is the average solar energy received per unit time on a unit area held perpendicular to the Sun's rays at the top of the atmosphere: about 1.4 kW m⁻², or 1400 J s⁻¹ m⁻². By the time it reaches the surface under a clear sky it is about 1 kW m⁻². Set an area and a time.

Intensity used
—
E = I × A × t
—
Energy
—
The worked example in the book: 1 m² for one hour at 1 kW m⁻². Set the sliders there first.
Work each one out.

India lies in the tropical and sub-tropical regions and receives abundant sunlight all year, which is why insolation matters so much here: it drives the southwest monsoon, and it offers enormous potential for solar power. Even a fraction of the Thar desert, covered in panels, could supply India's electricity needs.

Anna Mani mapped it first
India's pioneering atmospheric scientist measured solar insolation across the country in the 1950s. With S. Rangarajan she published Solar Radiation Over India in 1982 — the country's first insolation atlas. The large-scale solar deployment happening now is built on those measurements.
05Albedo: what bounces backActivity 13.2 · Table 13.145 XP

The fraction of solar radiation a surface reflects is its albedo — from the Latin for whiteness. High albedo surfaces stay cool because they reflect; low albedo surfaces heat up because they absorb. Pick a surface.

Albedo
—
Reflected
—
Result
—
Snow reflects most of what hits it. Black soil and ocean water absorb most of it. That single number explains a great deal about where the Earth is cold.

Snow and ice have high albedo and reflect a large proportion of incoming solar radiation, which is part of why polar regions are so cold. Black soil and ocean water have low albedo, absorb more, and are relatively warmer. Dark roads heat up faster than light-coloured surfaces, and dark clothes feel hotter than white ones in summer, for exactly the same reason.

The urban heat island
Cities are warmer than the countryside around them, in summer and at night. Concrete, steel, brick and asphalt absorb solar radiation and re-radiate the heat, warming cities more than rural areas. That raises demand for air conditioning, which stresses the urban ecosystem further. Rural areas and forests stay cooler through shade and plant transpiration.
06Why the poles are coldSection 13.1.2 · latitude and shape40 XP

The Sun's rays arrive as a parallel beam. Because the Earth is a sphere, that beam strikes different latitudes at different angles — and the same beam spread over a larger patch of ground delivers less energy to each square metre of it. Drag the latitude.

Latitude
—
Area lit
—
Energy per m²
—
One beam, one amount of energy. Only the size of the patch it lands on changes.

Radiation falling on the equatorial region is concentrated over a smaller area; near the poles the same beam is spread over a much larger one. That is why equatorial regions stay relatively warm all year while polar regions are much colder. Together with the tilt of the Earth's axis, which gives us seasons and changing day length, this uneven heating is what drives global winds and ocean currents.

If the Earth were a flat disc facing the Sun instead of a sphere, what would change?
The whole equator-to-pole temperature gradient comes from the sphere. A flat disc facing the Sun would be lit at one angle everywhere, so there would be no latitude gradient — and with no gradient there would be no pressure belts, no planetary winds and no ocean gyres.
Part 3 · The atmosphere
07Climbing through the layersSection 13.1.3 · Fig. 13.7, Table 13.245 XP

The air is held in place by the Earth's gravity and is mainly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%), with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour. It has a layered structure, and the temperature does something surprising as you climb. Drag upward.

Layer
—
Temperature
—
What is here
—
Watch the temperature line reverse direction at 12 km. That reversal is what keeps weather in the bottom layer.

Nearly all weather happens in the troposphere (0–12 km), which is heated from the Earth's surface below, so its temperature decreases with height at about 6.5 °C per kilometre. Warm air rises, and that drives winds and storms. The troposphere is tallest over the equator and shallowest over the poles.

In the stratosphere (12–50 km) the ozone layer absorbs UV and heats the air, so temperature increases with height. That inversion suppresses vertical mixing and calms the layer — which is exactly why weather stays confined below it, and why aircraft fly at its base. Above are the mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere, which play only a minor role in surface climate. Outer space begins at about 100 km.

The ozone hole, and the agreement that worked
Ozone shields life by absorbing harmful UV. Human-made chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), used in refrigerators and aerosols, destroyed ozone molecules faster than they formed, causing severe loss over Antarctica. The Montreal Protocol reduced CFC use and the layer is now slowly recovering — the clearest case there is of international scientific cooperation working.
08The blanket, and too much of itSection 13.1.3 · the greenhouse effect50 XP

The surface absorbs sunlight and re-radiates it as infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb that outgoing heat and stop it escaping to space. Without them the Earth would be too cold for life. Move the greenhouse gas level and watch what leaves.

Incoming absorbed
—
Heat that escapes
—
Surface
—
Slide to zero and the Earth freezes. Slide to the top and it becomes uninhabitable. The habitable band is narrow.

The atmosphere protects life in two ways. It partly absorbs incoming radiation — the ozone layer blocks harmful UV, and clouds and gases absorb some sunlight before it reaches the ground. And it traps outgoing heat: greenhouse gases like CO₂, CH₄ and water vapour absorb the re-radiated infrared and prevent it escaping into space. Without the atmosphere the Earth would be too cold to live on.

But excess CO₂ from human activities enhances the effect, causing global warming, which if left unchecked could make the Earth uninhabitable. Venus is the demonstration: it is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun, because Venus has an atmosphere and an uncontrolled greenhouse effect.

09Radiation and the airSections 13.1 to 13.1.335 XP

Tick where the statement is true.

Tap once for a tick, twice for a cross.

The last column is the one worth pausing on. Warming happens because the surface absorbs short-wave solar radiation and re-radiates it as long-wave infrared, which greenhouse gases then trap. Sunlight is not absorbed directly by CO₂ on the way in — the sequence matters.

Part 4 · Winds and currents
10The breeze that reverses at sunsetSection 13.2.1 · Fig. 13.845 XP

In mountainous regions the slopes and the valley floor do not heat and cool at the same rate — and that alone is enough to set the air moving. Switch between day and night.

Called
—
Warmer now
—
Air flows
—
Pick a time of day. The whole mechanism is one idea: warm air rises, and cooler air moves in to replace it.

By day, slopes facing the Sun heat more rapidly than the valley floor. Air over the slopes warms and rises, creating a low pressure region, and cooler air flows up from the valley to replace it — a valley breeze. After sunset the slopes lose heat faster and become cooler while the valley floor stays relatively warmer; air over the slopes becomes cooler and denser and flows down into the valley — a mountain breeze.

These daily reversals are familiar in Shimla, Dehradun and other Himalayan valleys. They influence weather, agriculture and daily life: they help regulate temperature and moisture and support soil and crop health. A grass-covered mountain and a bare rocky one would not give the same breeze, because they do not heat and cool at the same rate.

11Belts of pressure, right round the worldSection 13.2.2 · Fig. 13.950 XP

Run the same idea at planetary scale and it produces a fixed pattern of pressure belts and winds between the equator and the poles. Drag from the equator northwards.

Belt
—
Air is
—
At the surface
—
Four belts, alternating low and high, from the equator to the pole. Drag through all of them.

Near the equator, intense heating makes warm air rise, forming an equatorial low pressure belt. That air moves poleward at altitude, cools, becomes denser and sinks around 30° N and S, forming the sub-tropical high pressure belts. From there some air flows back along the surface towards the equator, completing one circulation cell. The rest moves poleward and rises again around 60°, where it meets cold air from the poles, creating the sub-polar low pressure belts. At the poles, very low temperatures make cold dense air sink, forming polar high pressure belts.

The Earth's rotation deflects these winds from straight paths, so planetary winds follow curved routes rather than running directly from high to low pressure: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

12Gyres, and a current that warms EuropeSection 13.2.3 · Fig. 13.1040 XP

Strong planetary winds drag the surface water of the oceans by friction, setting currents in motion. The Earth's rotation bends them into vast circles called gyres.

Showing
—
Rotation
—
Effect
—
Gyres rotate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern. Continents block and redirect them.

Besides wind, currents are driven by differences in temperature and salinity. Warm equatorial water travels along the surface towards the poles while colder, denser water flows back towards the equator through deeper levels. Water with lower salinity is less dense and stays near the surface; higher salinity water sinks and moves at depth.

Currents regulate climate and support life. By transporting heat from the equator towards the poles they reduce temperature differences across the planet. The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, flows towards north-western Europe and keeps many ports ice-free in winter even at high latitudes — which supports trade and commerce as well as a vast ecosystem, because currents also transport nutrients.

Part 5 · Matter goes round
13Water, and oxygenSections 13.3.1 and 13.3.435 XP

Energy flows through the Earth system and leaves. Matter does not — it cycles. Two of the four cycles first.

Cycle
—
Biggest store
—
Kept turning by
—
Pick a cycle and follow the loop round.

A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so climate change is already altering the water cycle — heavier rain in some areas and drought in others. Melting glaciers add water to rivers and raise sea levels, threatening coastal cities like Mumbai and Chennai. Sudden intense rainfall means more run-off, which erodes soil, and less infiltration, which reduces groundwater recharge and makes agriculture harder in dry months.

14Carbon, fast and slowSection 13.3.2 · Fig. 13.13 and 13.1445 XP

Carbon is the backbone of life — every protein, carbohydrate, fat and DNA molecule contains it. It moves between the atmosphere, biosphere, geosphere and hydrosphere on two wildly different timescales.

Showing
—
Timescale
—
CO₂ in air
—
Two cycles run on the same atom. One takes days; the other takes millions of years. Burning fossil fuels connects them.

In the fast cycle, over days to years, plants convert atmospheric CO₂ into glucose by photosynthesis; respiration returns it; decomposition returns what is left when organisms die. In the slow cycle, over millions of years, dead plants and animals are buried and converted to coal, oil and gas. Burning those fuels releases that carbon back as CO₂ on a very short timescale — which is precisely the problem.

Human activities have raised atmospheric CO₂ by about 35 per cent since 1960, from 315 ppm to 420 ppm — an unprecedented rise in the history of human civilisation. Some CO₂ is necessary to keep the Earth warm enough for life; the balance is what is critical. Excess CO₂ intensifies the greenhouse effect, melts glaciers and Arctic sea ice, raises sea level and brings more extreme weather. In India it may mean more intense monsoons, since warmer air holds more moisture.

Where the carbon actually is
Carbon is about 49% of the dry weight of living organisms. Of the total global carbon, 71% is in the oceans — and the atmosphere holds only about 1%. That is why the ocean matters so much as a regulator, and why a warmer ocean absorbing less CO₂ is such a serious feedback.
15Nitrogen: 78% of the air, and uselessSection 13.3.3 · Fig. 13.1545 XP

Nitrogen is essential for proteins and nucleic acids, and the atmosphere is the largest reservoir of it on Earth. But N₂ gas is so unreactive that plants and animals cannot use it directly. Follow the conversions that make it usable.

Step
—
Who does it
—
Becomes
—
Five steps, and bacteria do almost all of them.
Put the conversions in order, starting from nitrogen gas in the air.

Lightning also fixes a tiny amount of atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen oxides. But today most nitrogen is fixed artificially by the Haber-Bosch process, which makes ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen and produces most of the fertilisers in use. This "bread from air" enabled India's Green Revolution and feeds billions — more than half the nitrogen atoms in the human body have been through it. The reaction is energy intensive, using around 1–2% of global energy, and overuse of fertilisers has degraded soil and water.

That overuse adds excessive nitrogen as nitrates to rivers and lakes, causing algal blooms that deplete oxygen and kill fish. The process is called eutrophication, and it threatens water bodies and coastal fisheries.
